idea: For our 45-minute afterschool club, grades 6-8, teach a single-session Arduino stoplight with a pushbutton, using kits we already own.

assessment.summary: A single-session Arduino stoplight with a pushbutton for grades 6-8 using existing kits is a well-matched, low-risk afterschool project with clear grade fit, safe 5V electronics, and strong AI-authoring value. The main problem is scope: building and coding three LEDs plus a button input from scratch in 45 minutes is unrealistic unless the session is trimmed or students have prior Arduino experience.

grade_level_fit.notes: Grades 6-8 explicitly stated. Breadboarding LEDs with current-limiting resistors and writing simple digitalWrite/delay and digitalRead logic is squarely within middle-school reach, especially with a wiring diagram and starter sketch.

materials_feasibility.notes: Prompter states kits are already owned, and standard Arduino starter kits contain everything needed (Uno-class board, breadboard, jumpers, red/yellow/green LEDs, 220-330 ohm resistors, tactile pushbutton, USB cable). Not stated: how many kits exist relative to student count, and whether laptops with the Arduino IDE (or a web editor with driver access) are available and pre-installed.

instructor_capability.notes: No specialist expertise required. A non-specialist can run this after building the circuit once themselves and rehearsing the upload workflow; the only real prep burden is knowing common failure modes (reversed LED polarity, wrong COM port, missing pull-down/INPUT_PULLUP on the button).

ai_assistance_value.notes: High value. Claude can author the starter sketch, a commented state-machine version, wiring diagrams described step by step, a debugging cheat sheet, extension challenges (pedestrian crossing, blinking yellow, timing changes), and an exit-ticket worksheet.

time_scope_fit.notes: 45 minutes is too tight for the full arc as described if students start from zero: kit distribution, breadboarding four components, IDE setup/upload, plus button logic and debugging typically runs 75-90 minutes with grades 6-8. Prior Arduino experience of the group was not stated, which is the deciding fact.

safety.notes: 5V USB-powered, low-current circuit with no heat, chemicals, or sharp tools. Only routine cautions: no shorting the 5V rail to ground, always use a current-limiting resistor with each LED, unplug USB before rewiring.

pedagogical_alignment.notes: Genuine build with real decision points (LED sequencing, timing values, how the button interrupts the cycle) and authentic debugging. Risk of collapsing into recipe-following if the 45-minute crunch forces a fully pre-written sketch and pre-wired board; preserve at least one open design choice for students.

open_questions: Have these students used Arduino before (uploaded a sketch, built a breadboard circuit), or is this their first exposure? This determines whether 45 minutes is viable.
How many working kits are available and what is the expected student count / students per kit?
Are laptops available with the Arduino IDE (or Arduino Cloud Editor plus USB drivers) already installed and tested, or does setup have to happen during the session?
Does the owned kit specifically include a tactile pushbutton and 220-330 ohm resistors, or will those need to be sourced?
suggested_changes: Trim the single 45-minute session to a 3-LED stoplight cycle only (no button), and move the pushbutton crosswalk feature to a second session or an extension challenge for fast finishers.
Alternatively, keep the pushbutton but pre-wire or pre-stage the breadboards (LEDs and resistors already placed) so class time goes to coding and testing rather than assembly.
Pre-install and test the Arduino IDE on all laptops before the session, and verify one board uploads successfully on the actual club machines.
Provide a working starter sketch that blinks a single LED, and have students extend it to three LEDs with their own chosen timings, so productive struggle survives the shortened scope.
Confirm kit count and set a fixed pairing plan (2 students per kit maximum) so every student gets hands on the breadboard.
